endorsements.quote: clinicians will need new competencies for co-navigating patient trust in AI, managing misperceptions, and intervening when machine outputs conflict with clinical judgment 26 – 28 .

unlisted_practices: Base AI regulation on risk differentiation between high-risk diagnostic AI and low-risk administrative tools, keeping it proportionate so it does not stifle innovation.
Evaluate AI systems through independent, perpetual external auditing and real-world testing rather than solely internal metrics or simulations.
Design AI with relational, human-centered principles (tone, timing, feedback) so it supports rather than replaces clinician-patient interaction.
Optimize medical AI across multiple technical, economic, and moral objectives rather than single proxy metrics.
Provide AI literacy education fostering critical engagement with algorithmic systems from an early age.
Harmonize global AI governance standards while remaining sensitive to national contexts.
Include policymakers and regulators in practitioner-informed regulatory discussions to close the governance gap.

screen.reason: The paper introduces a conceptual framework ('Seven Deadly Sins of AI in Medicine' and corresponding cardinal virtues) for ethical governance and deployment of AI in medicine, validated via a stakeholder opinion poll.
